title: Sets, Relations, and Functions
tagline: The vocabulary of mathematics: sets define collections, relations capture structure between elements, and functions are the maps that connect every computation.

sections.content:
Sets, relations, and functions are the building blocks of every mathematical structure you will encounter in computer science. A **set** is an unordered collection of distinct elements: {1, 2, 3}, the set of all strings, the empty set ∅. **Set operations** — union (∪), intersection (∩), difference (\), complement, and Cartesian product (×) — let you combine and compare collections. These operations correspond directly to SQL joins, type system unions, and database schema design.

A **relation** on sets A and B is any subset of A × B — a set of ordered pairs. Relations model connections: 'x divides y', 'person x is friends with person y', 'state x transitions to state y'. **Functions** are special relations where each input maps to exactly one output. The classification of functions — injective (one-to-one), surjective (onto), and bijective (both) — is fundamental to counting, cryptography, and type theory.

sections.title: Sets as Guest Lists, Relations as Seating Charts
sections.content:
Imagine a party. The **set** of guests is a list — no duplicates, order doesn't matter. Union is merging two guest lists; intersection is guests invited to both parties; difference is guests at party A but not B; Cartesian product pairs every guest from A with every guest from B (useful for round-robin tournament scheduling).

A **relation** is the seating chart — a set of pairs (guest, table). A guest can sit at multiple tables (not a function). A **function** is a stricter seating rule: each guest is assigned to exactly one table. An **injective** function means no two guests share a table. A **surjective** function means every table has at least one guest. A **bijective** function is a perfect matching: every guest to exactly one table, every table has exactly one guest — this is the concept underlying encryption keys, hash collisions, and counting arguments.

**Equivalence relations** are relations R on a set A that are reflexive (aRa), symmetric (aRb → bRa), and transitive (aRb ∧ bRc → aRc). They partition a set into **equivalence classes** — disjoint subsets where every element in a class is related to every other. Modular arithmetic is the canonical example: 'a ≡ b (mod n)' is an equivalence relation that partitions integers into n classes {0, 1, …, n-1}. Union-Find (disjoint set) data structures implement equivalence classes efficiently.

**Partial orders** are reflexive, antisymmetric (aRb ∧ bRa → a=b), and transitive. They model hierarchies: subset ⊆, divisibility, lexicographic order. A **total order** additionally has comparability (every pair is related), like the natural ordering of integers.

**Function properties**: f: A → B is **injective** (one-to-one) if distinct inputs give distinct outputs: f(x) = f(y) → x = y. It is **surjective** (onto) if every element of B is mapped to by some element of A: ∀b ∈ B ∃a ∈ A f(a) = b. It is **bijective** if both — there is a perfect one-to-one correspondence between A and B, implying |A| = |B| for finite sets. Bijections are invertible; the inverse function f⁻¹ maps each b back to its unique a.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: JavaScript's Set provides union, intersection, and difference via spread and filter. The Cartesian product is a double loop producing all pairs. The injective check scans for duplicate images (O(n) with a Set). The surjective check verifies every codomain element is reachable. f(x) = 2x on {1,2,3} is bijective onto {2,4,6}; f(x) = x² on {-1,0,1} fails injectivity because f(-1) = f(1) = 1.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Bijection = same size.** For finite sets, f: A → B is bijective if and only if |A| = |B|. This extends to infinite sets: Cantor showed the integers and rationals have the same cardinality (a bijection exists) but the reals do not (no bijection from integers to reals — the 'diagonal argument'). In CS, bijections power hash table design (perfect hashing), cryptography (key spaces), and counting arguments. Whenever you need to show two collections have the same size, construct a bijection.

items: **Sets** are unordered collections of distinct elements; key operations are union (∪), intersection (∩), difference (\), Cartesian product (×), and power set P(A) with |P(A)| = 2^|A|.

A **relation** on A × B is any subset of pairs; **equivalence relations** (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) partition sets into equivalence classes — the foundation of modular arithmetic and Union-Find.
**Partial orders** (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive) model hierarchies like ⊆ or divisibility; **total orders** add comparability (every pair is related).
A **function** f: A → B is injective if distinct inputs give distinct outputs, surjective if every output is reachable, and **bijective** (invertible) if both — implying |A| = |B| for finite sets.
**Function composition** (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) is associative; compositions of injections are injective, compositions of surjections are surjective.

quiz.question: Which set operation produces elements in A or B but not both?
quiz.explanation: Symmetric difference A △ B = (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B) — elements that are in exactly one of A or B. Union includes elements in either or both. Intersection includes only elements in both. Difference A \ B includes elements in A but not B.

quiz.question: If |A| = 3, how many elements does the power set P(A) have?
quiz.explanation: |P(A)| = 2^|A| = 2³ = 8. The power set contains all subsets including ∅ and A itself. For A = {a,b,c}: {}, {a}, {b}, {c}, {a,b}, {a,c}, {b,c}, {a,b,c} — eight subsets.

quiz.question: An equivalence relation must satisfy which three properties?
quiz.explanation: An equivalence relation is reflexive (aRa), symmetric (aRb → bRa), and transitive (aRb ∧ bRc → aRc). These three properties ensure it partitions the set into disjoint equivalence classes. Antisymmetric (instead of symmetric) defines a partial order.

quiz.question: Function f: {1,2,3} → {a,b,c,d} with f(1)=a, f(2)=b, f(3)=c. Is f injective? Surjective?
quiz.explanation: f is injective: distinct inputs (1,2,3) map to distinct outputs (a,b,c) — no two inputs share an output. f is NOT surjective: element d ∈ {a,b,c,d} is not the image of any input. For a bijection you'd need |domain| = |codomain|, but here |domain|=3 < 4=|codomain|.

quiz.question: What is the Cartesian product A × B if A = {1,2} and B = {x}?
quiz.explanation: A × B = {(a,b) | a ∈ A, b ∈ B}. With A={1,2} and B={x}: {(1,x), (2,x)}. The size is |A| × |B| = 2 × 1 = 2. Note the order matters: A × B ≠ B × A in general.

quiz.question: A partial order differs from a total order in that a partial order:
options: Allows pairs of elements that are incomparable (neither aRb nor bRa)
Requires that every element relates to itself via symmetry
quiz.explanation: In a partial order, some pairs may be incomparable. For example, subset inclusion on {∅, {1}, {2}, {1,2}}: {1} and {2} are incomparable — neither ⊆ the other. A total order adds comparability: for every pair (a,b), either aRb or bRa (or both if a=b).

quiz.question: If f: A → B is bijective, which statement is true?
options: f⁻¹: B → A exists and is also bijective
f must be a linear function
quiz.explanation: A bijection is invertible: the inverse f⁻¹: B → A maps each b to its unique preimage a. Moreover, f⁻¹ is itself bijective. For finite sets, bijectivity implies |A| = |B| (not greater or less). The function need not be linear — any bijective mapping qualifies.

quiz.question: The equivalence classes of the relation 'a ≡ b (mod 3)' on integers are:
options: Infinitely many classes, one per integer
quiz.explanation: Mod 3 partitions integers into exactly 3 equivalence classes by remainder: class [0] = multiples of 3, class [1] = numbers leaving remainder 1, class [2] = numbers leaving remainder 2. These are disjoint and cover all integers — the defining property of equivalence classes.

quiz.question: Function composition (g ∘ f)(x) means:
options: f(g(x)): apply f first, then g
g(f(x)): apply f first, then g
quiz.explanation: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)): f is applied first, then g is applied to the result. The notation reads right-to-left. Composition is associative — (h ∘ g) ∘ f = h ∘ (g ∘ f) — but not generally commutative: g ∘ f ≠ f ∘ g.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT a valid relation on {1,2,3}?
quiz.explanation: A relation on A is a subset of A × A — a set of ordered pairs. A triple (1,2,3) is an element of A × A × A, not A × A. The other options are all valid subsets of {1,2,3} × {1,2,3}. Option A is the identity relation (also an equivalence relation), B has transitivity, C is symmetric.
